# Results -- Study 538 (Industry-Relative-Reversal) on the real monthly tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Recipe: each month, form two
competing one-month reversal signals from last month's return -- **RAW** (sort on the total
return, the Jegadeesh 1990 / [Study 329](../../329-one-month-reversal/) signal) and
**INDUSTRY-RELATIVE** (sort on the return minus the stock's own GICS-sector mean,
Hameed-Mian 2015 / Da-Liu-Schaumburg 2014). Long the bottom quintile (losers), short the
top quintile (winners), hold one month, rebalance. Pinned against a one-month-gap
(bid-ask-bounce) variant, a **placebo industry-label-shuffle null**, a beta decomposition,
a sub-period split, a turnover/cost sweep, and a synthetic positive control that proves the
engine isolates the within-industry component.
**Survivorship-biased**: the basket is current S&P 500 names projected backwards -- all
results are upper bounds. As-of **2026-06-26** (the panel is trimmed to the last complete
month, 2026-05-31; the in-progress June bar is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | Shape | Fingerprint (last row) |
|--------|--------|-------|------------------------|
| yfinance monthly (adj close), fixed 6-sector survivor basket | 1990-01-31 -> 2026-05-31 | 437 months x 54 tickers | `bbd55e07b990` |

Basket: 54 large-cap names, six GICS sectors -- Tech (14), Health (12), Financials (10),
Energy (6), Staples (6), Discretionary (6). ~11 names per quintile, 435 rebalance months.

## skip=0 -- RAW vs INDUSTRY-RELATIVE (the head-to-head)

| Signal | Spread | HAC *t* | Hit-rate | Spread beta |
|--------|--------|---------|----------|-------------|
| RAW (total return, Study 329 signal) | -11.0 bps/mo = -1.32%/yr | **-0.41** | 48.0% | 0.073 |
| **INDUSTRY-RELATIVE (within-sector)** | **+9.5 bps/mo = +1.14%/yr** | **+0.56** | 50.3% | 0.149 |

- The **industry-relative signal flips the sign and beats the raw signal** (+9.5 vs -11.0
  bps/mo) -- exactly the Hameed-Mian (2015) prediction that the reversal lives in the
  *within-industry* component and the raw signal dilutes it with the non-reversing
  industry move.
- **But neither clears the inference bar.** The IRR spread HAC *t* = **+0.56** is the right
  sign and the right ranking, yet far below 2.0 on this 54-name survivor basket. The
  industry adjustment helps; it does not manufacture significance.

## The industry adjustment is *real* (placebo), but the effect is small

### Placebo -- industry-label shuffle null (200 shuffles)

We randomly permute the sector tags across tickers 200 times and rebuild the IRR signal. If
"industry-relative" were an empty relabelling, the real IRR *t* would sit in the bulk of the
shuffled distribution; if the adjustment uses genuine industry structure, it sits in the tail.

| Quantity | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Shuffled IRR *t*: mean / sd | -0.48 / 0.36 |
| Shuffled IRR *t*: 5th / 95th pct | -1.05 / +0.06 |
| **Real IRR *t*** | **+0.56** |
| **Placebo p (shuffled *t* >= real)** | **0.005** |

The real industry-relative *t* sits **above the 99.5th percentile** of the shuffled null
(p = 0.005): demeaning by the *true* sectors is decisively better than demeaning by random
groups. The within-industry framing is doing genuine work -- the within component really is
where the reversal concentrates. The effect is simply too small (on a 54-name basket) to
cross *t* = 2 in level.

### Bid-ask-bounce variant (skip=1, a one-month gap)

| Variant | RAW spread / *t* | IRR spread / *t* |
|---------|------------------|------------------|
| skip=0 (adjacent) | -11.0 bps/mo / -0.41 | +9.5 bps/mo / +0.56 |
| skip=1 (one-month gap) | +10.4 bps/mo / +0.40 | +27.5 bps/mo / +1.33 |

Unlike Study 329's raw reversal (which *dies* with a one-month gap -- the bid-ask-bounce
signature), the industry-relative spread is actually *larger* one month out (+27.5 bps/mo,
*t* = +1.33). It is not a pure microstructure artefact -- but +1.33 still does not clear the
bar, so it is suggestive, not certified.

## Sub-period decay (IRR spread, skip=0)

| Period | Spread | HAC *t* | n months |
|--------|--------|---------|----------|
| 1990-2002 | +15.1 bps/mo | +0.43 | 154 |
| 2003-2014 | -4.2 bps/mo | -0.15 | 144 |
| 2015-2026 | +17.7 bps/mo | +0.70 | 137 |

No sub-period clears the bar. The IRR spread is mildly positive in the 1990s and the most
recent decade, flat in between -- a faint, unreliable edge throughout, not a sharp
publication fade. This is a far cry from the strong original in-sample academic result;
on a thin survivor basket the industry-relative reversal is a whisper.

## Tradability -- turnover and cost sweep

The IRR loser quintile turns over **~76.6%** one-way each month (a one-month signal is
almost entirely refreshed every rebalance). Costs: one-way x NAV across both legs,
round-trip, plus a flat 50 bps/yr borrow on the short (winner) leg.

| One-way cost | Net spread (+borrow) | Net HAC *t* |
|--------------|----------------------|-------------|
| 0 bps  | +5.4 bps/mo | +0.31 |
| 5 bps  | -10.0 bps/mo | -0.59 |
| 10 bps | -25.3 bps/mo | -1.49 |
| 20 bps | -55.9 bps/mo | -3.32 |

**Break-even one-way cost: ~3.1 bps** (before borrow). At ~77% monthly turnover a
sub-2%/yr gross edge cannot survive even retail-grade costs: the net spread is negative
by 5 bps and significantly *loss-making* by 20 bps. Untradable.

## Positive control -- the engine isolates the within-industry component

On the deterministic synthetic tape (`data.synthetic_panel`, a common non-reversing
industry factor plus a planted within-industry one-month reversal), the same engine reads
~0 on the null and recovers the planted signal -- and crucially the **industry-relative
sort is cleaner than the raw sort**, because the raw sort is diluted by the (non-reversing)
industry move:

| Planted within-industry reversal | RAW spread *t* | IRR spread *t* |
|----------------------------------|----------------|----------------|
| 0.00 (null) | -0.08 (~0) | +0.70 (~0) |
| +0.04 | +30.98 (+113%/yr) | **+69.46 (+127%/yr)** |
| +0.08 | +67.27 (+241%/yr) | **+144.52 (+259%/yr)** |

The engine is a faithful detector and, by construction, the industry-relative sort *beats*
the raw sort when the reversal is within-industry. So the real-tape "right sign, right
ranking, sub-2 *t*" result is a fact about this thin survivor **market**, not a broken
method.

## Verdict

- **Signal -- WEAK.** The industry-relative reversal does what the literature says: it
  flips the raw signal's sign, beats it (+9.5 vs -11.0 bps/mo), survives a one-month gap
  (where the raw bid-ask-bounce reversal dies), and the industry adjustment is decisively
  real on the placebo (label-shuffle p = 0.005). **But the level is tiny**: IRR HAC
  *t* = +0.56, no sub-period clears 2.0. Directionally confirmed, statistically not
  certified -- WEAK, not REAL. Survivorship-biased upper bound on a 54-name basket.
- **Tradability -- MIRAGE.** ~77% one-way monthly turnover; break-even ~3.1 bps; net spread
  negative by 5 bps and a significant loss by 20 bps. A sub-2%/yr gross edge at 100% monthly
  refresh cannot be traded.
- **Does industry-adjustment beat raw? -- CONFIRMED.** On both the real tape (IRR +9.5 vs
  RAW -11.0 bps/mo; IRR survives skip=1, RAW does not) and the synthetic control (IRR
  *t* = 69 vs RAW *t* = 31 at the same planted within-reversal), the within-industry sort is
  the better signal. The mechanism is right; the magnitude, on this basket, is just too
  small to trade.
